headline: Village Elects Mayor by Coin Toss; Rest of World Quietly Asks Why It Made This Complicated
subheadline: After a dead-even vote high in the Andes, two rivals settled the election with a single flip of a coin — a process observers note was faster, cheaper and arguably more transparent than most democracies.
author: Clementine Reyes-Holt, Global Affairs Correspondent
seoTitle: Peru Village Elects Mayor by Coin Toss | The Daily Absurd
seoDescription: Satire: a Peruvian village settled a tied mayoral election with a coin toss. The rest of the world is taking notes.
sourceEvent: In Conima, near Lake Titicaca, Peru, a tied mayoral election was legally settled by a coin toss under Peruvian law; the winner said 'I always wanted to win, and God decided it.'

social.x: A Peruvian village just settled a tied mayoral election with a coin toss. Total cost: one coin. Total lawyers: zero. Democracy has questions to answer.
social.facebook: Two candidates, same number of votes, one coin. Peru may have accidentally invented the world's most honest electoral system.
social.instagram: Heads: mayor. Tails: gracious in defeat. The whole thing took eleven seconds. #satire #peru
altHeadlines: Electoral Commission Replaced by Single 50-Centavo Coin
Coin Toss Decides Election; Coin Immediately Favours Incumbency

body:
High in the Peruvian Andes, the village of Conima has conducted what political scientists are calling 'the most efficient election in recorded history', after a tied mayoral vote was settled — entirely legally — by the toss of a coin.

The two candidates, having received exactly the same number of votes, agreed to trust in luck, as Peruvian law permits. The coin was flipped. A mayor emerged. The entire process took eleven seconds, cost one coin, and produced a result both candidates accepted, a sentence that has never previously appeared in journalism.

"I always wanted to win, and God decided it," said the newly sworn-in mayor, thereby becoming the first politician in history to concede that his mandate was 50% chance.

The international reaction has been one of quiet awe. In Washington, an aide reportedly stared at the news for several minutes before whispering 'imagine'. In Brussels, officials called an emergency meeting to discuss forming a committee to examine whether a task force could study the procedure. The meeting is scheduled for March 2031.

Critics point out that coin-toss governance has drawbacks, chief among them that it removes the traditional nine months of recounts, lawsuits and televised men pointing at maps. 'It denies the people closure,' said one election-night presenter, 'and more importantly, it denies us thirty-six hours of premium coverage.'

Bookmakers, meanwhile, have hailed the system as 'finally, an election with honest odds'.

At press time, the Conima council had announced its first act of governance: deciding whether lunch would be empanadas or soup. It was settled by rock, paper, scissors. Sources confirm the soup faction has conceded.
